title: Should juries decide complex fraud trials?

turns.speaker: Craig
turns.text: That fraud trial ran fourteen months. Twelve jurors gave up over a year of their lives to it.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: And the proposal is judge-only trials for anything above a certain complexity threshold.

turns.speaker: Blaise
turns.text: Which is where I get uncomfortable, because complexity is defined by the people who benefit from the change.

turns.speaker: Craig
turns.text: That's a bit cynical. Somebody has to draw the line.

turns.speaker: Blaise
turns.text: Somebody does. My point is that fraud is precisely the offence where defendants can afford to make things complicated.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: So difficulty becomes a defence strategy and then a reason to remove the jury.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That's an unattractive incentive however you look at it.

turns.speaker: Craig
turns.text: The practical case is real though. Fourteen months excludes anyone who can't take that off work, so the jury isn't representative anyway.

turns.speaker: Blaise
turns.text: That's the strongest argument and it's an argument for paying jurors properly rather than for abolishing them.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: There's a middle option some countries use. A judge sits with two lay assessors who have relevant expertise.

turns.speaker: Craig
turns.text: Which keeps a public element without asking twelve strangers to learn accounting.

turns.speaker: Blaise
turns.text: I'd want to see how those assessors get chosen before agreeing. That's where it would go wrong.

points: A fourteen-month fraud trial prompts proposals for judge-only trials above a complexity threshold.
Blaise objects that complexity would be defined by those who benefit, and fraud defendants can afford to make cases complicated.
Nadia notes this creates an incentive to make trials difficult in order to remove juries.
Craig's practical argument is that long trials exclude anyone unable to take time off work, so juries are unrepresentative.
Blaise responds that this argues for paying jurors properly rather than abolishing juries.
Nadia offers a middle option of a judge sitting with expert lay assessors, which Blaise accepts conditionally depending on selection.
